title: Writing Has a Framework Problem
author: Amarylise Bessey
summary: Amarylise Bessey responds to Trisha Jha's Knowledge is Power II report on Australian teachers' professional knowledge gap, asking a different question: what knowledge do teachers actually draw on when they teach writing? She notes that reading reform has increasingly specified the knowledge behind teachers' decisions, while writing discussion still centres on practices, pedagogies and frameworks such as AERO's Writing Instruction Model. A framework can say that modelling and feedback matter, but it cannot say what to model or what feedback a particular student needs, and those calls rest on professional judgement and therefore knowledge. She draws on Young-Suk Kim's integrated view of reading and writing, listing oral language, vocabulary, morphology, syntax, discourse knowledge, self-regulation and background knowledge as an existing base. She concludes that the real gap may be that no widely accepted account of the knowledge underpinning writing decisions has yet been described.
points: Teaching writing is a stream of small decisions about what to respond to first, and good decisions depend on professional knowledge rather than on following a program.
Reading reform specified the knowledge teachers need, but writing discussion has focused on practices and frameworks, leaving the knowledge beneath the decisions underdescribed.
Frameworks cannot determine what to model or what feedback a given student needs, which requires diagnosing whether the barrier is ideas, sentences, spelling, structure or self-regulation.
Kim’s integrated view suggests a writing knowledge base can be built from overlap with reading knowledge such as oral language, vocabulary, morphology, syntax and background knowledge.
The more interesting reading of Knowledge is Power II is that writing education has not yet described the professional knowledge teachers use, rather than that teachers have gaps.
quotes: Effective teaching is not simply the delivery of strategies or programs. It involves making hundreds of instructional decisions, often with incomplete information and in highly complex classroom contexts.
One of the major achievements of these reforms has been their attempt to specify knowledge rather than simply prescribe practice.
A framework can tell us that modelling is important. It cannot tell us what to model for a particular student, at a particular point in time, in response to a particular learning need.
A framework can tell us that feedback matters. It cannot determine whether a student needs feedback on ideas, sentence construction, text structure, spelling, or self-regulation.
Kim’s work is particularly useful because it encourages us to move beyond questions of strategy and towards questions of understanding.
These are not simply pedagogical questions. They are questions about professional reasoning. And professional reasoning depends upon professional knowledge.
Yet these developments sit alongside a striking omission: no widely accepted account of the professional knowledge that underpins teachers’ decisions about writing.
